links.outcome: Effect of 'Made with AI' source labels on perceived message effectiveness of health ads
links.effect: Labeling showed no significant association with any of 5 PME measures (chi2 0.10 to 4.19; all P > .20); sensitivity analysis of the 462 who passed the manipulation check was similar.
links.quote: Labeling the ads as AI-generated or created by an official health agency had no significant association with PME among young people.

unlisted_practices: Youth codesign with iterative prompt refinement (few-shot, multi-prompt, manual text-image integration) to generate public health campaign ads
Noninferiority comparison of AI-generated ads against existing health agency ads

links.outcome: perceived message effectiveness vs existing ads
links.effect: Noninferior on all 5 measures; better discouraging vaping b=0.09, attention b=-0.15, convincingness b=-0.18; all noninferiority P<.001.
links.quote: AI-generated ads received better ratings for discouraging vaping (b = 0.09; 95% CI, 0.01 to 0.17), attention-grabbing qualities (b = -0.15; 95% CI, -0.26 to -0.03), and convincingness (b = -0.18; 95% CI, -0.30 to -0.07) (all P for noninferiority tests <.001).

links.effect: No significant association with any of 5 PME measures: χ2 values 0.10 to 4.19; all P > .20.
links.quote: Source labeling showed no significant association with PME scores (χ2 values ranging from 0.10 to 4.19; all P > .20).
Results from the sensitivity analyses, which was limited to only the 462 participants (75%) who passed the manipulation check, produced similar results (eTable in Supplement 1 ).

links.outcome: perceived message effectiveness across source labeling conditions

links.quote: Likelihood ratio tests comparing models with and without labeling conditions revealed no significant association of source labeling with any of the 5 PME measures (χ 2 values ranging from 0.10 to 4.19; all P > .20).
